Period schedule:

Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Tribute: Understanding Sacrifice and Tone

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.201): theme, tone, and poetic devices — paired discussion.
Let us think and reflect (p.202): extract questions on antonyms, soldiers' quality, and harsh weather.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem "My Dear Soldiers" aloud at an unhurried pace while students follow in their textbooks (p.199–200). A brief activation invites students to name one person in their lives — a soldier, firefighter, or rescue worker — who serves selflessly; two or three responses are shared aloud.

Using "Let us discuss" (p.201), the class works through the poem's theme and tone as a guided whole-class discussion. The teacher draws attention to the repeated contrast between "we" and "you," the yogi simile, the wind-chimes metaphor, and the alliterative pairs, asking students to explain the effect of each device in their own words.

Students work in pairs on selected questions from "Let us think and reflect" (p.202): identifying opposite words from the extract beginning "When we are all asleep", giving evidence of harsh weather from the same lines, and selecting the quality of dedication from the given choices. Pairs share one finding each before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's second-person address ("You") is central to its emotional force; prompt students to feel its directness rather than treating it as a stylistic label. A common pitfall is confusing the yogi simile (spiritual discipline on lonely terrain) with a statement about religion — the poem_appreciation_summary clarifies that it signals focused, selfless endurance. Students who do not finish the extract questions may revisit them while reading the poem independently.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Companion Poem and Reciting with Feeling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.203): predict and fill blanks; listen to "A Soldier's Pride" and verify.
Let us speak (p.203): paired practice then group recitation of "My Dear Soldiers" with expression.

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes or displays the gapped text of "A Soldier's Pride" (p.203). Students work individually for a quick paired exchange to predict the eight missing words — reasoning from rhyme scheme and theme — before any listening begins.

The teacher reads "A Soldier's Pride" aloud at a steady pace (transcript, p.224). Students listen and correct their predicted answers. A short whole-class check confirms the eight words; the teacher asks students to name which images in the listening poem echo those in "My Dear Soldiers."

Following the guidance in "Let us speak" (p.203), pairs practise reciting "My Dear Soldiers" — observing the marked pauses, varying volume for tenderness versus pride, and maintaining posture. After an unhurried rehearsal period, three or four groups of eight to ten take turns reciting aloud; the class offers one word of feedback per group.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task is most effective when students commit to predictions first — the gap between prediction and heard word sharpens attention to rhyme and meaning simultaneously. In the recitation phase, students from backgrounds where public performance feels uncomfortable should be invited to participate in the group rather than singled out; the poem's prayerful closing lines offer a naturally softer entry point for hesitant voices. The poem's alliterative pairs ("snowy / season," "defending / deserts") are useful anchors for discussing where to place vocal stress.
materials: Textbook — p.203 (listening cloze and speaking guidance)

periods.activity_title: Writing in Two Forms: Acrostic Poem and Gratitude Note

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.204): compose an acrostic poem using a chosen word.
Let us write (p.204): draft a 50-word gratitude note beginning "Dear Bravehearts."

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the sample SOLDIER acrostic from "Let us write" (p.204) aloud and briefly explains how each line must open with its letter AND connect to the poem's world — terrain, weather, sacrifice, or prayer. Students choose their own word (SOLDIER, NATION, BRAVE, or YOUTH) and jot two or three line ideas before drafting.

Students write their acrostic poems independently. The teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck by pointing to specific images in the poem — the marshes, the wind chimes, the scorching rays — as raw material for their lines. Two volunteers share their completed acrostics aloud; the class identifies which line they find most vivid.

Students draft the 50-word gratitude note ("Let us write," p.204) beginning "Dear Bravehearts, I would like to…". The teacher models one opening sentence on the board, then students write independently. Pairs exchange notes, read each other's aloud in a whisper, and offer one suggestion before writers make a final revision within their own minutes.

periods.teacher_notes: Both tasks draw directly on the poem's emotional core — the acrostic makes imagery concrete, and the gratitude note practises a functional form within the same theme. A common pitfall with acrostics is filling each line mechanically with an adjective alone; encourage students to use the terrains, seasons, and actions from the poem to build full phrases. Students who complete both tasks quickly may attempt a second acrostic using a different word.
materials: Board or display surface for teacher model sentence

periods.activity_title: Collocations, Terrains, and Honouring Soldiers Beyond the Page

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.202): identify terrains from the box — two items do not apply.
Let us learn (p.203): fill in collocating words from given brackets.
Let us explore (p.205): design a badge of honour with a logo and slogan.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.205): find a poem or story in your mother tongue about soldiers' bravery and prepare a short presentation.

time_bands.activity: Working through "Let us learn" (p.202–203), the class first identifies which words in the terrain box (ghats, river, plateau, delta, bay, peninsula, mountains) name physical features actually mentioned or implied in the poem, and which two do not apply — the teacher asks students to point to the poem line that justifies each choice. Students then complete the five collocation blanks (p.203) individually and check in pairs, with the teacher drawing attention to how phrases like "treading the lonely expanses" and "scorching sun" from the poem model the same word-pairing logic.

Students open "Let us explore" (p.205) and begin designing their badge of honour for soldiers on a sheet of paper — sketching a logo that captures one image from the poem (terrain, wind chimes, or the yogi simile) and composing a short slogan of no more than six words. After an unhurried making period, four or five students hold up their badges and read their slogans aloud; the class names which poem image each badge draws on. The teacher notes the homework task of finding a regional-language poem or story about soldiers' bravery for a future presentation.

periods.teacher_notes: Collocations are best taught by returning to the poem's own phrasing — "scorching sun's sweltering rays" and "lonely expanses" are model collocations the class has already encountered, so the blanks exercise should feel like pattern recognition rather than guesswork. A common pitfall in the terrain task is including "river," which appears in the box but not among the poem's listed terrains; redirect students to the specific lines listing valleys, deserts, marshes, seas, and heights. The badge task is open-ended; students with limited drawing confidence should be reassured that a bold slogan carries equal weight to an elaborate logo.
materials: Textbook — "Let us learn" p.202–203 and "Let us explore" p.205
Blank paper or card for badge design

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic tone, theme, and literary devices using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tribute poem by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam — tone, yogi simile, wind-chimes metaphor, second-person address, soldiers' sacrifice.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 199 beginning "Treading the lonely expanses as yogis". Which of the following best describes why the poet compares soldiers to yogis in this line?

options.label: A
options.text: To show that soldiers practise meditation and religious rituals in the mountains.

options.label: B
options.text: To suggest that soldiers move through remote terrain with focused, selfless discipline.

options.label: C
options.text: To indicate that soldiers are physically frail and need spiritual support.

options.label: D
options.text: To compare the loneliness of soldiers with the isolation sought by ascetics for personal peace.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the spiritual discipline implied by the simile with literal religious practice.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads the simile as implying weakness rather than austere strength.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Partially captures isolation but misapplies it as a personal choice rather than a duty-driven condition.

items.source_context: Tribute poem by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam — tone, yogi simile, wind-chimes metaphor, second-person address, soldiers' sacrifice.
items.item_stem: The poem "My Dear Soldiers" consistently uses "you" to address the soldiers and "we" to refer to ordinary citizens. Explain how this repeated contrast between "you" and "we" shapes the poem's tone and reinforces its central theme of collective gratitude and sacrifice. Support your answer with at least two moments from the poem.

expected_elements: Identifies the "you/we" contrast as creating intimacy and directness.
Links "we sleep" versus "you guard" to collective gratitude.
Names the prayerful closing ("We pray for you") as the tone's peak.
Connects the contrast to the theme of sacrifice given by soldiers for citizens.

items.item_stem:
Listen to "A Soldier's Pride" and decide whether each statement below is true or false. Write True or False and give one word or phrase from the poem to justify your answer.
1. The soldiers' duty is described as something that can be left unfinished.
2. The poem says soldiers march through stormy skies and blazing heat.
3. The poem states that soldiers fight only during the daytime.

options.text: The soldiers' duty is described as something that can be left unfinished.
The poem says soldiers march through stormy skies and blazing heat.
The poem states that soldiers fight only during the daytime.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — the poem says "it must be done," showing the duty is non-negotiable and cannot be left unfinished.
2. True — the poem uses the exact phrase "stormy skies and blazing heat."
3. False — the poem says soldiers guard "both night and day," not only during the daytime.

items.item_stem: In "A Soldier's Pride," the final stanza says soldiers fight "to keep our hopes and dreams alive." In your own words, explain what this line suggests about the relationship between a soldier's service and the lives of ordinary citizens. Use one more detail from the poem to support your answer.

expected_elements: States that soldiers' service protects citizens' future aspirations.
Connects "hopes and dreams" to everyday civilian life and freedom.
Uses a second detail, such as guarding "both night and day" or defending India "till the very end."
Shows understanding that the soldier's sacrifice enables ordinary life to continue.

items.item_stem: Recite the stanza beginning "Windy season or snowy days" from "My Dear Soldiers" to a partner. Use a softer, solemn volume for the weather lines and a stronger, proud voice for the line "You are there guarding all the time awake." Your partner will listen and tell you one thing you did well and one thing to improve.

expected_elements: Recites the stanza clearly with correct word order.
Varies volume between the weather lines and the guarding line.
Maintains a steady pace without rushing.
Listens and gives specific, kind feedback to partner.

items.item_stem: The poet closes "My Dear Soldiers" with a prayer: "We pray for you brave men!! May the Lord bless you all!!" Imagine you are the speaker of the poem and you are addressing a gathering on Armed Forces Day. Speak two to three sentences in the voice of that speaker, explaining why you feel the soldiers deserve the nation's deepest gratitude. Give at least one specific reason drawn from the poem — a terrain, a season, or a line about sacrifice.

expected_elements: Speaks in first person as the poem's grateful citizen-speaker.
Names at least one specific terrain or season from the poem.
Expresses a reasoned opinion about why gratitude is deserved.
Uses appropriate formal register for a public address.

items.item_stem: Write a short note of gratitude (40–50 words) addressed to the soldiers of India. Begin with: "Dear Bravehearts, I would like to…" Your note must mention at least one specific hardship from the poem — a terrain, a weather condition, or the sacrifice of youth — and express your admiration sincerely.

expected_elements: Opens correctly with "Dear Bravehearts, I would like to…"
Names at least one specific hardship from the poem (terrain/weather/youth).
Stays within the 40–50 word limit.
Closes with a sincere expression of admiration or a prayer.

items.item_stem: Compose an acrostic poem using the word BRAVE. Each line must begin with the correct letter AND connect to an idea, image, or emotion from "My Dear Soldiers" — such as the terrains soldiers guard, the seasons they endure, or the sacrifices they make. You may use the poem's world freely but must write your own original lines.

expected_elements: Each of the five lines begins with the correct letter (B, R, A, V, E).
At least three lines draw on a specific image or idea from the poem.
Lines are phrases or full sentences, not isolated adjectives.
The poem conveys admiration, sacrifice, or the soldier's duty overall.

items.item_stem: Match each terrain word from Column A with its correct description from Column B. The terrain words are all drawn from the world of "My Dear Soldiers" or the vocabulary box studied alongside it.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A (Terrain) | Column B (Description) |
|---|---|
| Valley | A wide, flat, elevated stretch of land |
| Desert | A low area of land between hills or mountains |
| Marsh | A vast, dry, sandy or rocky landscape |
| Plateau | Wet, low-lying land that is often waterlogged |
| Mountain | A high, steep landform rising above the surrounding area |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Valley–c, Desert–c (see answer_key), Marsh–d, Plateau–a, Mountain–e

answer_key.right: A low area of land between hills or mountains
A vast, dry, sandy or rocky landscape
Wet, low-lying land that is often waterlogged
A wide, flat, elevated stretch of land
A high, steep landform rising above the surrounding area

items.source_context: Terrain types from box (ghats, plateau, mountains etc.); collocations from poem — scorching sun, lonely expanses, dense forest.
items.item_stem: The poem "My Dear Soldiers" uses strong collocations — word pairings that belong naturally together — such as "scorching sun" and "lonely expanses." Choose ONE of these two collocations and write two sentences of your own that use it correctly. Your sentences must show that you understand both the meaning of the collocation and the feeling it creates in the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any two grammatically correct sentences that use the chosen collocation accurately and show awareness of its emotional weight — for example, sentences that place "scorching sun" in a context of endurance or hardship, or "lonely expanses" in a context of isolation and duty.

items.source_context: Badge of honour for soldiers — self-designed logo and slogan drawing on poem imagery.
items.item_stem: Design a badge of honour for the soldiers celebrated in "My Dear Soldiers." Your badge must include: (a) a simple logo or symbol that represents one image from the poem — such as wind chimes, a mountain, a yogi figure, or the sun — and (b) a slogan of no more than six words that captures the poem's spirit of gratitude or sacrifice. Write or draw your design on paper and write one sentence below it explaining why you chose that image.

expected_elements: Badge includes a clearly drawn or described logo linked to a poem image.
Slogan is six words or fewer and expresses gratitude or sacrifice.
Explanatory sentence connects the chosen image to the poem's meaning.
Overall design reflects an understanding of the poem's admiring, prayerful tone.

items.source_lo: Student creates a symbolic artefact that extends the poem's themes of honour and service beyond the text.
items.source_context: Badge of honour for soldiers — self-designed logo and slogan drawing on poem imagery.
items.item_stem: The poem "My Dear Soldiers" honours soldiers who guard mountains, deserts, marshes, seas, and air borders — giving their youth to the nation. Think of a public space in your town or city (a park, a school entrance, a railway station) and plan a small memorial display that would help ordinary people remember this sacrifice. Describe your display in a short paragraph (60–80 words): name the space, say what you would put there (a plaque, a mural, an installation, a statue, or something else), and explain which line or image from the poem inspired your choice.

expected_elements: Names a specific public space and states why it is appropriate.
Describes the display clearly — type, content, and scale.
Links the design to at least one line or image from the poem.
Shows that the purpose is public awareness and collective gratitude.
